skills.name: order-custom-poster
skills.description: Use this when the user wants a physical poster, print, or canvas made from an image they made, from print-size check through approved checkout and tracking.
skills.content:
---
name: order-custom-poster
description: >-
  Use this when the user wants a physical poster, print, or canvas made from an
  image they made, from print-size check through approved checkout and tracking.
---
# Order a custom poster

Turns a finished image into a real printed poster. Each order is a purchase: nothing is paid for without the user's explicit Approve on that exact order.

## 1. Confirm what to print
- Which image (exact file), the size (for example 18x24, 24x36 or A1), the finish (matte, gloss, satin or canvas), whether they want a frame, and the quantity.
- Only print images the user made or has the rights to. No real people's likenesses and no copyrighted characters or logos they don't own.

## 2. Check the file fits the print
- Required pixels = inches x dpi. Aim for 300 dpi, and never go under 150. 24x36 at 300 dpi needs 7200x10800.
- If the file is too small, upscale it first, then recheck the size.
- Match the aspect ratio to the poster size. Show the user the crop or the letterbox before ordering, and never crop silently.
- Export a print file: sRGB, highest-quality JPG or PNG, plus any bleed the printer asks for (often 0.125 in a side). Keep important content out of the bleed.
- Confirm the printer's upload size and format limits.

## 3. Pick the printer and get a real quote
- Run SearchPlugins for a print-on-demand connector first. Otherwise use the printer's website in the box browser (load the box-desktop skill and the site's playbook if there is one).
- Pick a reputable poster printer that ships to the user's address. If the user names one, use it.
- Upload the print file, set the size, finish and quantity, and use the printer's own proof or preview to check the crop.
- Get the shipping address from the vault (vault skill). Never ask for an address that's already saved.
- Go up to the final review step, so the grand total with tax and shipping is known. Screenshot the proof and the total.

## 4. Approval, every order
- Send the proof screenshot, then an Approve / Cancel widget: item (image, size, finish, quantity), merchant, grand total, and the estimated delivery date.
- Pay only after Approve, following the purchases skill (wallet order, vault card, bank-check handling). Never carry an approval over from another order or an earlier message.
- Cancel or no answer means stop, and say it wasn't ordered.

## 5. After the order
- Verify the confirmation page or email before saying it's placed. If a checkout step failed, check order history before retrying.
- Log the spend as the purchases skill says.
- Tell the user the order number, total and expected delivery. Offer a routine to watch tracking until it's delivered.

## Never
- Never order without an Approve on this exact order.
- Never put card details anywhere but the merchant's checkout.
- Never claim a refund or guarantee you didn't read on the printer's page.

skills.name: wallpaper-pack
skills.description: Use this when the user wants one big image cut into exact-size wallpapers for phones, desktops, ultrawides, tablets or a digital photo frame.
skills.content:
---
name: wallpaper-pack
description: >-
  Use this when the user wants one big image cut into exact-size wallpapers for
  phones, desktops, ultrawides, tablets or a digital photo frame.
---
# Wallpaper pack

Cuts one large master image into pixel-exact wallpapers for every screen the user names. Crops only, never stretches, and the user approves the crops before anything is packaged.

## 1. Confirm the source and the sizes
- Which image (exact file, the full-res master, not a preview) and which devices. If they don't say, offer the default set below.
- Phone (portrait): 1179x2556, 1290x2796, 1080x2400, 1440x3200.
- Desktop: 1920x1080, 2560x1440, 3840x2160, 5120x2880.
- Ultrawide: 3440x1440, 5120x1440.
- Tablet: 2048x2732, 1668x2388, 2560x1600.
- Digital photo frame: 1920x1080, 1280x800, 1024x600 (ask the frame's native resolution if they know it).
- Ask for the focal point if the image has one obvious subject. Otherwise use smart crop.

## 2. Check the master is big enough
- For each size, the crop region must be at least the target pixels on both axes. If a target needs upscaling more than about 1.5x, upscale the master first (with the bot's upscale step) instead of enlarging small crops.
- Never change the aspect ratio by scaling one axis. Every output is crop then uniform resize.

## 3. Crop each size
- Focal point: given as a fraction of width and height (for example 0.5, 0.4). Center the crop window there and clamp it inside the image.
- Smart crop when no focal point is given: score candidate windows with an entropy or saliency map (Python with Pillow and numpy, or OpenCV saliency if available) and keep the highest scoring window.
- Largest window of the target aspect that fits, positioned as above, then a uniform Lanczos resize to exact size:
  `magick master.png -crop {w}x{h}+{x}+{y} +repage -filter Lanczos -resize {W}x{H}! -strip -quality 95 out/phone_1179x2556.jpg`
  (the `!` is safe here because the crop is already the exact aspect.)
- Phones: keep the subject out of the top ~12% (clock) and bottom ~8% (dock or home bar). Shift the window if it collides.
- Name files `<device>_<W>x<H>.jpg` (PNG if the image has flat graphics or text). Verify every file's dimensions with `magick identify`.

## 4. Contact sheet for approval
- Build one sheet showing every crop labeled with its size:
  `magick montage out/*.jpg -geometry 480x480+12+12 -label '%f' -background '#111' -fill white contact.jpg`
- Send the contact sheet and ask Approve / Adjust. If they adjust (move the focal point for one size, drop a size), redo just those crops and resend.

## 5. Package and deliver
- After approval: `zip -j wallpapers.zip out/*`, then deliver the zip plus a short list of sizes and which device each fits.
- Keep the master untouched.

## Never
- Never stretch or squash to fit an aspect ratio.
- Never package before the user approves the contact sheet.
- Never post or upload the pack anywhere the user didn't ask for.

skills.name: print-prep-check
skills.description: Use this when the user brings in an image file and wants to know if it will print well at a given size, or wants a print-ready export of it.
skills.content:
---
name: print-prep-check
description: >-
  Use this when the user brings in an image file and wants to know if it will
  print well at a given size, or wants a print-ready export of it.
---
# Print prep check

Inspects a file someone brings in, says plainly whether it will print well at the size they want, and produces the fixed export.

## 1. Get the file and the target
- The exact file, the print size (inches or cm, or a named size like A2 or 24x36), and the printer or product if known (their bleed and format rules win over defaults).

## 2. Read the file
- `magick identify -verbose file` (or Python Pillow) for: pixel width and height, embedded dpi tag, color space (sRGB, Adobe RGB, Display P3, CMYK), ICC profile name, bit depth, alpha channel, and file format.
- The embedded dpi tag doesn't matter on its own. Only pixels versus print size matter.

## 3. Work out the numbers
- Effective dpi = pixels / inches, per axis, after any crop to the print aspect. Report the lower axis.
- Aspect mismatch = image aspect versus print aspect as a percent. Say how much would be cropped (or letterboxed) and from which edges.
- Required pixels at 300 dpi = inches x 300 (for example 24x36 needs 7200x10800). With bleed, add bleed to each side first (0.125 in per side is a common default, so 24.25x36.25).
- Safe zone: keep text and key detail at least 0.25 in (about 6 mm) inside the trim line.

## 4. Verdict, in one line
- **Ready:** effective dpi of 300 or more (240 or more is fine for large posters viewed from a distance), aspect fixed, profile fine.
- **Upscale first:** 150 to 299 dpi. Upscale to the required pixels, then recheck.
- **Too small:** under 150 dpi even after a sensible 2x to 4x upscale, or the detail is too soft. Offer a smaller print size that would be ready, with its numbers.

## 5. Make the fixed export
- Convert to sRGB unless the printer asks for something else: `magick in.tif -profile sRGB.icc out.tif` (use the file's own profile as source; for CMYK input, convert through its embedded profile).
- Crop to the print aspect (show the crop first, never crop silently), add bleed by extending the edges (`-gravity center -extent` with mirrored or content-aware edges, not white bars unless the user wants a border).
- Flatten alpha onto the intended background color, 8-bit, highest-quality JPG or PNG/TIFF per the printer's limits. Set the dpi tag to the real value (`-density 300 -units PixelsPerInch`).
- Output a guide overlay preview showing trim, bleed and safe zone lines so the user can check placement.

## 6. Report
- Pixel size, effective dpi, aspect mismatch, color profile before and after, bleed and safe zone needed or not, the verdict, and the export file. Hand off to the poster-ordering skill if they want it printed.

## Never
- Never say a file is print-ready without doing the dpi math.
- Never crop or add bleed without showing the user the result.
- Never re-upload or share the user's file anywhere they didn't ask for.

skills.name: style-lock
skills.description: Use this when the user wants a series of giant images to share one consistent look (palette, grain, lighting, lens), or asks to add a new image to an existing series.
skills.content:
---
name: style-lock
description: >-
  Use this when the user wants a series of giant images to share one consistent
  look (palette, grain, lighting, lens), or asks to add a new image to an
  existing series.
---
# Style lock

Keeps a series of images looking like they belong together. The look lives in a style card saved next to the series, and every new image is checked against it.

## 1. Build the style card (first image of the series)
- Start from the image the user calls the anchor (or the first approved one).
- Save `style-card.json` and a readable `STYLE-CARD.md` in the series folder with:
  - **palette:** 5 to 8 hex values pulled with k-means on the anchor (Python Pillow and numpy or scikit-learn), each with its share of the image.
  - **tone:** luminance histogram summary (mean, p5, p50, p95), contrast, saturation mean.
  - **grain:** none, fine or heavy, plus the noise strength measured from a flat area.
  - **lighting:** direction, time of day, hard or soft, key-to-fill feel, color temperature.
  - **lens:** focal-length feel (wide, normal, tele), depth of field, perspective (eye level, aerial, isometric).
  - **rendering keywords:** the exact prompt phrases that produced the look, and the negative phrases.
  - **reference images:** file names of the anchor and any approved images, kept in `refs/`.
- Show the card to the user and get an OK before using it.

## 2. Make each new image with the card
- Start every prompt from the card's rendering keywords, lighting and lens lines, then add the new subject. Pass reference images when the tool supports it.
- Keep the same aspect, resolution target and upscale or detail settings as the series.

## 3. Check for drift after each image
- Extract the new image's palette and histogram the same way.
- Palette drift: for each card color, nearest new color by delta E (CIEDE2000). Flag if the average delta E is over about 10 or any main color is missing.
- Tone drift: flag if mean luminance moves more than about 8% or saturation more than about 15%.
- Grain: flag if measured noise is off by more than half.
- Make a side-by-side strip: anchor, new image, and both palettes as swatches.

## 4. Fix or accept
- If flagged, say what drifted in plain words ("warmer and lower contrast than the series"). Offer a regenerate with corrected keywords, or a light grade toward the card (curves and color balance, never repainting content).
- If the user likes the drift, update the card on purpose and note the change and date in `STYLE-CARD.md`.
- Add each approved image to `refs/`.

## Never
- Never change the card silently.
- Never copy a living artist's name or a brand's style as a keyword.

skills.name: zoom-reveal
skills.description: Use this when the user wants a short video or GIF that starts on a full giant image and zooms smoothly into one tiny detail, to show off how much detail it holds.
skills.content:
---
name: zoom-reveal
description: >-
  Use this when the user wants a short video or GIF that starts on a full giant
  image and zooms smoothly into one tiny detail, to show off how much detail it
  holds.
---
# Zoom reveal

Makes an 8 to 15 second clip (or a GIF) that opens on the whole image and glides into one small detail at native resolution. It only moves a camera over the real image: no new content is generated. The user posts it themselves.

## 1. Confirm the shot
- The full-res master (not a preview), the detail to land on (point at it, or give a fraction like 0.62, 0.31), the length (default 10 s), and formats: 1080x1920 vertical, 1920x1080 horizontal, or a GIF.
- Optional: hold times at start and end (default 1.5 s each), music (the user's own or royalty-free only).

## 2. Plan the camera
- Start window: the whole image fit to the output aspect (crop the long side, or pad with a blurred copy if the user wants the full frame visible).
- End window: centered on the detail and sized so one output pixel is about one master pixel (true native resolution). Never zoom past 1:1, which would just enlarge pixels.
- Ease: smootherstep (6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3) on the zoom, interpolated in log scale so the zoom speed feels constant. Center moves on the same eased curve.

## 3. Render
- Preferred: Python crop sequence on the master. For each frame at 30 fps, compute the window, crop with Pillow or OpenCV, Lanczos resize to output size, and pipe raw frames to ffmpeg:
  `ffmpeg -f rawvideo -pix_fmt rgb24 -s 1080x1920 -r 30 -i - -c:v libx264 -crf 16 -preset slow -pix_fmt yuv420p -movflags +faststart zoom_1080x1920.mp4`
- Quick option: ffmpeg zoompan on a pre-scaled copy (zoompan jitters at high zoom, so supersample the input 2x to 4x of output size and keep the expression smooth). Use the Python route for zooms over about 20x.
- For very large masters, read the master with a tiled reader (pyvips or Pillow with crops) rather than loading it whole in memory.
- GIF: 720 px wide, 15 fps, palette pass: `ffmpeg -i zoom.mp4 -vf "fps=15,scale=720:-1:flags=lanczos,split[a][b];[a]palettegen[p];[b][p]paletteuse" zoom.gif`. Keep it under about 15 MB.

## 4. Check and deliver
- Watch for jitter, banding and soft frames. Check the last frame is crisp at native resolution.
- Pull 3 stills (start, middle, end) and send them with the clip.
- Deliver the MP4s and GIF. Suggest an on-screen caption only if the user wants one.

## Never
- Never generate, paint in, or upscale new detail for the clip. Only the real pixels of the master.
- Never post, upload or schedule the clip. The user posts it.

skills.name: getting-started-mural
skills.description: Use this on Mural's first conversation with a new owner, to set up giant-image defaults before the first render.
skills.content:
---
name: getting-started-mural
description: >-
  Use this on Mural's first conversation with a new owner, to set up giant-image
  defaults before the first render.
---
# Getting started with Mural

Say in one line what Mural does: it makes giant images that hold up when you zoom in (8K to 16K, or print sizes), and turns them into wallpaper packs, prints and posters.

Then ask these one at a time, skipping any the owner already answered:
1. What do you mostly want big images for: wallpapers, prints and posters, or zoomable art?
2. Do you have a computer with a GPU you want to connect for faster upscales? If not, everything runs on Mural's own computer, which is slower but works.
3. Which devices should wallpaper packs fit by default (your phone, monitor, ultrawide, a photo frame)?
4. Any house style to lock in for a series (palette, grain, mood)? If yes, run the style-lock skill to save a style card.

With the answers:
- Save each preference as a short profile memory: the use, the default size, the devices, whether a GPU is connected. Never save addresses or card details in memory; those go in the vault.
- Offer to make the first image right away: "tell me what to make and how big."
